results.title: Hansen J-Test for Overidentification Calculator | MetricGate
results.content: The Hansen J-test (also known as the Sargan-Hansen test) is the standard diagnostic for assessing instrument validity in models estimated by Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) or two-stage least squares (2SLS) when there are more instruments than endogenous regressors. In an overidentified model, the extra instruments provide testable restrictions: if all instruments are valid, the sample moment conditions should be approximately zero. The J-statistic measures how far the sample moments deviate from zero, and a large value casts doubt on the validity of at least one instrument. Under the null that all instruments are valid, J converges to a chi-squared distribution with q - p degrees of freedom. The Hansen J-test (also called the Sargan-Hansen test) is a diagnostic for instrumental variables (IV) models estimated by Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) or two-stage least squares (2SLS). Under the null hypothesis that all instruments are valid, J follows a chi-squared distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of overidentifying restrictions (number of instruments minus number of endogenous regressors).

results.title: What is: Overidentification Test Explained
results.content: The Overidentification Test is a statistical procedure used primarily in the context of econometrics and structural equation modeling. This test is crucial for ensuring the reliability of the results obtained from models that rely on instrumental variables. ## Purpose of the Overidentification Test. The main purpose of the Overidentification Test is to evaluate the validity of the instruments in a model. There are several methods to conduct the Overidentification Test, with the most common being the Sargan test and the Hansen test. The Sargan test is based on the idea of using the residuals from the estimated model to check the validity of the instruments. When a model is overidentified, it provides an opportunity to test the validity of the instruments, which can enhance the credibility of the findings. In the field of data science, the Overidentification Test is particularly relevant when working with causal inference and predictive modeling. In summary, the Overidentification Test is a vital tool in econometrics and data analysis for validating instruments in overidentified models.

You have 4 tests you're asking about: Hausman test, Sargan test, a Wald test of exogeneity, and a Hansen J Test. To fix some notation, let $Z$ be a vector of instruments, and consider $Y = \beta\_1 X\_1 + \beta\_2 X\_2 + e$, where $X\_1$ are exogenous variables you include in the model, and $X\_2$ are endogenous, and you wish to use $Z$ instruments for $X\_2$. Before beginning, the TL;DR is that Wald and Hausmann test for exogeneity of $X$ (assuming exogeneity of $Z$), and Hansen's J and Sargan test for exogeneity of $Z$ (assuming you have more instruments than endogenous variables).

results.title: Hansen overidentification test: Significance and symbolism
results.content: # Significance of Hansen overidentification test. The Hansen overidentification test assesses the validity of instrumental variables. It tests the null hypothesis that the chosen instrumental variables are effective and reasonable. The test evaluates whether the moment conditional variables used in the estimation are jointly effective, accepting the null hypothesis if they are deemed valid. Synonyms: Overidentification test, Sargan test, J-test, Instrument validity. ## The concept of Hansen overidentification test in scientific sources Science Books. The Hansen overidentification test assesses the validity of moment condition variables in estimation. It tests if these variables are jointly effective, accepting the null hypothesis when tool variables are deemed reasonable. (1) It judges whether the moment conditional variables used in the estimation process are effective in general, with the original hypothesis that the variables are jointly effective. (1) The Hansen overidentification test accepts the null hypothesis that tool variables are effective, indicating that the choice of tool variables is reasonable.
